content: When antiretroviral therapy (ART) is initiated at maternal and child health (MCH) facilities, women who are on long-term ART must transition to HIV care facilities postpartum. Their medical records must also be transferred to ensure continuity of care. This necessitates that MCH facilities track ART services based on the time since ART initiation rather than antenatal care (ANC) visits, aligning with general ART data collection tools. If MCH facilities are not yet using tools harmonized with the national ART system, countries must carefully review and develop mechanisms to transfer data between patient monitoring systems. Such mechanisms are essential for proper monitoring of women on lifelong ART and for utilizing data to evaluate program performance. Even for women who are not eligible for lifelong ART and stop ART after the mother-to-child transmission (MTCT) risk period (Option B), it is recommended to adopt tools used for long-term ART monitoring, such as ART registers and facility-held client cards. Toxicity monitoring is also critical, as it is for all patients on antiretroviral drugs (ARVs), to detect adverse reactions in pregnant women and infants receiving PMTCT services. The effectiveness of PMTCT services depends on the consistent use of ARVs throughout the MTCT risk period. As guidelines for maintaining mothers on ART during this period are implemented, monitoring retention and adherence becomes increasingly important. However, monitoring ARV coverage during breastfeeding and assessing the final HIV status of exposed infants have been weak points in the cascade. Countries must invest in improving data completeness for these later stages of the cascade as they scale up PMTCT programs and work toward validating the elimination of mother-to-child transmission of HIV (EMTCT). All pregnant women initiating ART under Option B or B+ should receive ART IDs, be registered in the ART program, and have their information recorded in ART monitoring systems. To ensure quality care, countries implementing Option B and B+ should use ART cards or files to monitor all pregnant and breastfeeding women on ART. Women on Option B should continue to be followed in HIV care (pre-ART) after they stop breastfeeding, with regular CD4 monitoring to ensure timely re-initiation of ART when indicated. Treatment records and national ART IDs should be maintained to ensure continuity of data linkages for all pregnant and postpartum women on ART. ART retention should be monitored for all pregnant and breastfeeding women initiating treatment. Women who start ART at MCH facilities and later transfer to HIV care facilities postpartum should be assigned to an ART retention cohort based on their treatment initiation date, not the date they transferred to the HIV care facility. Retention monitoring should also include pregnant and breastfeeding women newly initiating ART, while those already on ART when they become pregnant belong to a different ART initiation cohort. Women who stop ART after completing the MTCT risk period should be classified under an additional outcome of completed ART for PMTCT to avoid lowering retention rates when calculating cohort outcomes. HIV-exposed infants must be followed to determine their outcomes. This includes reporting their final HIV status, which measures progress toward ensuring that all infants born to HIV-positive women are either confirmed HIV-negative or, if HIV-positive, linked to ART services. Many countries track HIV-exposed infants using registers or facility-held cards, identifying them at birth or during the first follow-up visit and monitoring them until their final outcome is established. This can be done using either paper-based or electronic systems, provided the information is organized by the infants' birth month for cohort reporting. The Global Plan recommends that all pregnant women be tested for HIV, regardless of the general population's HIV prevalence. However, in low-prevalence settings with limited resources, testing can focus on women at higher risk of HIV. Countries in such settings should assess coverage within high-risk groups, such as women who inject drugs or have partners who inject drugs, and monitor the proportion receiving PMTCT interventions along the cascade to ensure adequate access for this key population. High coverage of early virological testing of infants is critical for initiating ART early in children with confirmed HIV infection and for counseling efforts to prevent seroconversion in those with a negative early test result. Final MTCT transmission rates measure the percentage of HIV-infected infants among HIV-exposed infants born in the past 12 months. This indicator evaluates the overall rate of transmission during the MTCT risk period and serves as a validation criterion for EMTCT of HIV.
